  10. The intellects are absorbed in existence, like a letter that cannot stand alone as a meaning. Souls are like names: their existence is connected to their own selves and does not disappear into another. Flowing natural powers and changing bodies are like verbs, or acts. — س قده

    ↩

  11. One might object that this is the highest kind of human speech, yet the person here is listening and receiving, not speaking. First, he speaks with God by asking through his readiness to receive knowledge and understanding from Him; conversation goes both ways. Second, even though these words are first and directly attributed to God or to an angel, they can also be attributed to the soul, as something is attributed to what displays it. They descend from the soul’s inner self to its outward side, the intellect. — س قده

    ↩

  12. This refers to the prophets. For others, the Prophet said, “Among my community are those who are spoken to and inspired.” — س قده

    ↩

  13. Taken broadly, Ibn Arabi’s words include the general intellectual knowledge of the rational soul. But his way of speaking and the context suggest that he means the knowledge of people of the heart and the divine promptings received by those on the spiritual path. They describe four kinds of inward prompting. A divine prompting, sometimes called a “knock on the heart,” never errs; it can be recognized by its strength and the way it cannot be pushed aside. An angelic prompting, or inspiration, urges a person toward something required or recommended. A prompting from the self, or an impulse, serves the person’s own interests. A satanic prompting, or whisper, urges a person away from what is right. God says, “Satan threatens you with poverty and commands you to do what is shameful.” These promptings can be hard to distinguish in matters where either choice is allowed. What goes against a person’s own desire is more likely to come from the first two; what agrees with it is more likely to come from the last two. By God’s help, a sincere person with a clear heart and attention turned to the truth can tell the difference. — س قده

    ↩

  14. Far from it! A report from the noble descendants of the Prophet says: “The Holy Spirit tasted the first fruits from the gardens of Ṣāqūra in our gardens.” — س قده

    ↩

  15. By “the Book,” he means the lowest level of the books written on heavenly tablets: the world of bodies. He reads “There is nothing fresh or dry that is not in a clear Book” as referring to literal opposites such as fresh and dry. — س قده

    ↩

  16. This means the tablet of breath—nafas, with a vowel on the f—and breath or air taken without restriction, as belonging to the soul—nafs, with the f unvowelled. In the first case, the book was treated as something separate from the soul. In the second, the forms written on the air or on paper are counted as existing through the rational soul. — س قده

    ↩

  17. It may seem that the passage first calls the breath or air a writer, then says the rational soul is the maker. At this lower level, the breathing soul makes the images and writes them on what receives them. — س قده

    ↩

  18. When the light of reality appears, nothing else has independent existence, much less a relation to God of either kind. Any relation that assumes separation is only the relation of reality to appearance, or else no real relation at all. This is why Avicenna says that the First has no relation to things; rather, things are related to Him. If things are the subject of the statement, God is their necessary ground, so they must be related to Him. But if God is the subject, things vanish because their existence is borrowed, and no relation remains. The verse “His are the creation and the command” does not prove an ordinary relation. It may mean that He is the preserved source and foundation of all, or that all things receive existence from Him. The better proof is that the one who gives something cannot lack what He gives. — س قده

    ↩

  19. This is also reported from the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī. The sages say that times and things in time relate to higher principles as the present moment does, and places and things in place as a point does. Events that follow one another in time all exist together in eternity. They explain this with a rope or piece of wood, colored differently along its length, passing in front of an ant whose narrow field of sight cannot take it all in. The colors appear to the ant one after another, but you see them all at once because your sight can take in the whole length. This applies when we look at the world’s forms and what receives them. But if we look at its meaning and existence, there is no extension or sequence at all. Existence has no parts, so it has no size, quality, measure, or number that could divide it into past, present, and future. There is no absence or presence, years or eternities, beginning or decay, return or recurrence. All of these apply only to the things that receive existence and to the forms in which it appears. The Persian verse says: “The water in this stream has changed many times, yet the moon and stars remain in its reflection.” — س قده

    ↩

  20. In both the outer world and the human inner world, there are four things: an inward Throne and Footstool, and their outward forms. In the outer world, the inward ones are the universal intellect and universal soul; the outward ones are the outermost sphere and the sphere of the fixed stars. In the human inner world, the inward ones are the inner heart, or detailed intellect, and the inner chest, or imagination. Their outward forms are the pine-cone-shaped heart and the brain. — س قده

    ↩

  21. The effect that reaches the storehouse of imagination is the image in the faculty itself. The lower effect mentioned here is the image in the subtle bodily spirit, which carries the imaginative faculty and displays it. — س قده

    ↩

  22. This refers to the circular path of the words. When the ear hears what the tongue says, the words return to their source and circle back on themselves, like the creative words through which things come to be. For this reason, some may prefer speaking remembrance of God aloud to silent remembrance, though silent remembrance is better in some respects. — س قده

    ↩

  23. “Good words” means the complete words: the simple, higher intellects in the upward order of existence. Good action—the religious law and the path of life—raises them. But the meaning that best supports the author’s point is that all beings are God’s words, considered in their luminous aspect. “Good action” then means their inner and outward movements toward greater completion. In this sense, creation itself worships God, as He says, “Your Lord has commanded that you worship none but Him.” This does not conflict with the fact that some beings turn away from Him in their religious conduct. — س قده

    ↩

  24. Just as a servant in the ordinary sense owns nothing, and everything in his hands belongs to his master, so the true servant’s being, attributes, and actions belong to the Lord of all masters. This follows from the unity of God’s essence, attributes, and actions. God is called the All-Merciful here because His mercy reaches everyone, while His special mercy is for those who believe in and know His oneness. “He has counted them one by one”: just as a final sum gathers all the separate numbers, God’s knowledge gathers all scattered beings in a simpler, higher way, and nothing lies outside it. “Each will come to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection”: when beings rise from the things that receive them and stand before the One, each is stripped of what is foreign to its own reality. At a minimum, this means leaving behind the worldly body and its attachments—in short, the limits of nature. Complete freedom from matter belongs only to the closest servants of God. A Persian verse says: “Today, yesterday, the day before, and tomorrow—all four become one in tomorrow.” This return to the All-Merciful takes place only in human form, since the human being is the gateway to God and the straight path to Him. The Qur'an guides people to what is most upright: to reflect God’s greatest name. Since God’s giving never ends, every natural being reaches the natural human being and enters through this gateway; all strongholds reach the greatest stronghold, and all villages reach the mother city. Mulla Sadra adds another way to understand this: beings enter the human being through their many relations to him, in his imagination and in the connected worlds of dominion and intellect. In short, when the perfect human being reaches the highest end, all beings reach it with him. This does not mean that each kind of being fails to reach its own Lord and is not gathered to God along with that Lord. — س قده

    ↩

  25. This passage concerns detailed knowledge, which gives rise to many things within unity, and mercy as an attribute, which gives rise to mercy in action. He is not speaking of God’s essential knowledge at the level of absolute oneness, or of His essential speech, which is simple and one. Although that knowledge contains all good things in a single, complete act of knowing, that is not the subject here, as his words make clear. — س قده

    ↩

  26. “Like them” may refer only to the number of earths matching the seven heavens, or it may mean that the earths are heavens too. Things are present in the mind through their own realities; what distinguishes one thing from another is also connected to what they share. The phrase may instead refer to the soul, heart, intellect, and the remaining levels of the human being, which are counted as seven, as will be explained later. In that reading, the unseen world of God’s command descends between these levels. — س قده

  27. “Two days” may mean the moment that has passed—the moment of passing away—and the moment that is coming—the moment of coming into being. Every changing thing in nature is in this state.   28. The Tablet may be the Tablet of Decree, where detailed knowledge is held—the world of the governing principles of different kinds, each letter containing all the letters of creation.   29. “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord” can be understood in several ways. Whoever knows the Prophet, who has a greater claim on believers than they have on themselves, knows his Lord, because the Prophet said, “Whoever has seen me has seen God.” The Prophet’s spiritual reality is the Universal Intellect, the fullest manifestation of God; in his all-embracing nature, he displays God’s Greatest Name. Or it may mean that whoever knows his own soul, created in the image of the All-Merciful and able to embody all the divine names when fully developed, knows his Lord. Knowing an effect as an effect, or a sign as a sign, is knowing its cause and what it points to—especially when the effect is a mirror of its source and has no independent standing. Or it may mean that whoever recognizes his own helplessness and knows that all power belongs to God knows God’s power and its reach. Whoever sees his own ignorance—once an empty mirror and blank page, later adorned with knowledge from God, the Wise and Knowing—knows God’s knowledge of all things, general and particular: “They do not encompass anything of His knowledge except what He wills.” Whoever knows himself as a servant, poor and owning no existence, quality, or action of his own, knows God as Lord, Master, and Self-Sufficient. A fourth reading is that whoever sees how his small world contains all levels—spiritual and bodily, angelic and satanic, with something in him like an angel, a sphere, a plant, an animal, and a devil—knows how the great world contains every level, from the smallest speck to the tiniest particle. A fifth reading describes something impossible: if a limited, ever-changing person could know the full reality of his own self, whose states and aspects cannot be counted, he would know the full reality of his Lord. But that cannot happen. In short, God has a hidden reality that no creature can grasp, and a manifest side known through Him. The soul too has a hidden reality beyond our grasp and a manifest side through which its powers and levels are known. A Persian verse says: “Knowing your soul is no small matter; know God, and you will know what it is.” — س قده

    ↩

  30. This difference between the Qur'an and the other books follows the difference between their messengers: God gave some messengers a higher rank than others. Since our Prophet is the last in both the order of existence and the line of prophets, no intermediary remains between him and God. The Qur'an is therefore God’s speech, and Gabriel’s role in bringing it down in portions does not contradict this. Other prophets had one or more intermediaries. The two conditions that make speech direct—its independence from what receives it and its direct dependence on the true speaker—were fully and steadily present in the Prophet, so no possible being could surpass him. God says, “Remain upright as you have been commanded.” — س قده

    ↩

  31. “God’s own speech” means that “God’s” qualifies “speech.” It does not mean that the Qur'an is speech but not a Book. As we have already seen, every speech is also a Book in one respect. — س قده

  32. The earlier distinction between speech and Book was based on whether they depend on matter. This distinction between Qur'an and Criterion is broader: it concerns what is one and what is many. The many may be different kinds of things or ideas, as with different intellects or divine names and attributes; or it may lie in different levels of existence, which vary in strength. The word “Qur'an” comes from a root meaning “to gather,” as in the verse, “Its gathering and its recitation are upon Us; when We recite it, follow its recitation.” The speech sent down to our Prophet is the Universal Intellect, his station and spiritual reality: the whole order of intellects that move the heavens and earth, from their beginnings to their ends. This speech is Qur'an in that it gathers things together; it is Criterion in that it distinguishes their kinds and levels. — س قده

  33. Whatever appears to the senses is perceived, whether it comes from outside or from within. Some followers of the philosophers go beyond saying that the Prophet’s reality connects with the angel’s reality. They say he also connects with the angel’s subtle form through imagination. They do not reduce this to an empty dream: they say the image comes down from the higher Tablets and reflects what is there, like the images in a true dream. Yet this account still falls short. The inner powers are like mirrors facing one another. When an image appears in imagination, it is also reflected in the common sense, which is like a mirror with two faces: one receives images from the outward senses, and the other receives what comes from the higher Tablets or from the imagination. Once we know that the image passes from the inner worlds to the illuminated imagination, then to the common sense, and from there to the senses, how could it fail to be truly seen? The Prophet’s intellect is above the other intellects, and his senses are more luminous than ordinary senses. — س قده

    ↩

The next words refer to the angels of the Tablets. — س قده

  35. The angel also has a subtle aspect that relates to the lower world. Its reality at the high station appears to the Prophet as a pure form in the world of subtle images. That is what is meant by its ascent and descent; it does not mean that it moves through space. The Qur'an says, “The angels and the Spirit descend,” and, “The command descends between them.” Many similar verses express the same idea. — س قده

  36. When the holy spirit of a saint, or someone below a prophet, speaks with angels while awake, the person’s powers do not follow the spirit as fully as a prophet’s powers do, because the saint’s spirit is not as strong as the Prophet’s. The powers remain caught up in sensory distractions, and the spirit cannot pull them away completely. When the Prophet’s spirit meets the angels in sleep, by contrast, his powers follow it, despite his seeming daze, and see what it sees. He is also awake in the natural world: he sees the angel’s form with his senses and hears its voice, recognizing it as an angel. This is one of the marks of prophecy. — س قده

  37. Written, spoken, mental, and outward existence are all appearances of one reality, whether in its full form or its subtle counterpart. A shadow is not separate from what casts it, a name is not separate from what it names, and a subtle form reflects the reality it represents. In brief, the Qur'an has three forms: the written copy between its covers, and the created signs in the outer world and within the soul. Whoever reads any one of these properly is, in a sense, reading the other two. — س قده

Those who lean more toward existence, with a stronger sense of oneness, are among the prophets and saints who draw near to God. The mind also separates qualities, amounts, positions, and other features that are mixed together in ordinary things. — س قده

  53. This means the intellects, which are God’s speech and true word. — س قده

  54. This means how the intellects become universal souls, which are God’s Book, and how they descend into open hearts.   56. The point is that the world beyond the senses contains everything found here, including all five senses, in a form suited to that world. Each sense is reached by a matching inward sense. In the same way, he can taste, smell, and touch what ordinary people cannot. The Prophet said, “I spend the night with my Lord; He feeds and gives me drink.” He also said, “I can smell the breath of the Most Merciful from the direction of Yemen,” and, “I felt the coolness of his fingertips between my breasts.” These reports point to it. In short, when a prophet or saint leaves ordinary awareness, he perceives through inward senses, each suited to what it knows. — س قده

When viewed as linked to their universal souls, they are pens that write on those tablets. — س قده

  63. Change takes place only on the two Tablets of Erasure and Confirmation: the unseen record and its visible counterpart. — س قده

Some people, especially those who combine deep knowledge with spiritual practice, can bring together both kinds of vision. — س قده

  65. This applies to the Qur'an as it exists in the world and within the human soul.     ↩

  66. This is clearer when applied to the Qur'an within the human soul than when applied to the written Qur'an, though the verse can include both. People were spiritually dead until God brought them to life by sending the Prophet, completing the work through the saint, and sending down the Qur'an. They were guided by its light. — س قده

    ↩

  67. This definition appears in The Healing and other works on divine philosophy. Wisdom is the best kind of knowledge because it gives certainty, not mere imitation. Other fields often rely on assumptions about their subjects, if not in every step then at least in accepting that their subjects exist. Divine philosophy has a leading place because its subject is existence itself, which is pure good; it studies God, His qualities and acts, the angels brought near to Him, and other beings that support the order of existence. Its goal is to make a person’s mind like the world and to reach true happiness. Its starting points are proofs that give lasting certainty. Its subject, goal, and starting points are all the best. The things it knows are therefore the best things to know. — س قده

    ↩

  68. This applies if wisdom means the highest form of direct knowledge, in which what is known is present to the knower. God alone has this knowledge in its fullest form, so wisdom is His gift. — س قده

    ↩

  69. The author relies here on the rule that higher causes are not completed by lower things, as his wording suggests. So “they had not already reached before acting” should mean prior in any sense, not only earlier in time. Separate higher causes do not gain perfection from actions that necessarily follow from their own nature. Their actions are blessings that flow from their being to what is below them. They have no goals in lower things for their own sake; if they did, those effects would complete them. Their goal is their own essence if nothing stands above them, as is true only of God, or a perfection above them, as is true of the separate intellects. Through their actions, the intellects imitate God by giving good, without needing the action or its results. This is pure generosity. That does not mean they are forced to act. They know their actions and approve of them because those actions fit their natures. An action of this kind is not coerced. Even if their actions follow necessarily from their natures, they still arise from knowledge and approval and are therefore chosen. — ط مد ظله

    ↩

  70. In short, providence brings together three things: knowledge, being a cause, and approval. We can clarify this by looking at what it means for us to take care over something. A person takes care to make an action happen, or to make it as complete as possible, without letting some other concern—more urgent, more loved, or more important—distract them from doing it. When we are busy with major matters, we may neglect small ones, either by not doing them at all or by not giving them all the care they need. If we give a small matter the same attention as a great one, or carefully manage all its needs and details as we would in a great matter, that is providence. We neglect small matters because we compare things. If two actions are required, one more important than the other, we may compare them, treat the more important one as the only real duty, and then neglect the less important one. Yet without that comparison, both would still be duties, and we would attend to the small one just as we attend to the large one. When we do not compare them, we know each action as it is: something required of us and suited to our nature. That is providence. It includes knowing the thing, causing it, and approving it because it fits the doer’s nature. God knows each thing as it is, without comparison or anything else weakening or changing that knowledge. He is the highest cause of every cause and its effects, and those effects fit His essence. So He has providence over all things. As this explanation shows, providence is normally an attribute of action: the fit between an action and its doer is understood from the action. But because that fit can be traced back to something in the essence, it can also be described as an attribute of essence. We can say that God’s essence knows things and causes them in a way that makes their effects fit Him. — ط مد ظله

  75. The power that perceives the harmful cause is not the power that suffers from it. The person’s sense of touch, which needs the sun’s warmth, cannot perceive the cloud. So the cloud is not itself judged evil by the power that perceives it; what is judged evil is the loss of health and warmth. The sense that can see the cloud is not harmed by it, while the sense that is harmed does not perceive it. If the cloud were evil in itself, it would make the perceiving sense suffer.   77. The reply does not seem to resolve the problem. First, the objection is broader than direct sense perception. The severed limb is only an example. Second, it is hard to say that sense perception is always direct awareness of the thing itself when the senses often make mistakes about the outside world. Saying that all knowledge is direct in some deeper way does not help, because that concerns knowledge as it is in itself, not whether it matches what exists outside us. The problem can instead be answered this way: the mental image that causes pain is not evil insofar as it perfects the person’s knowledge. In that respect it is something good that exists. But insofar as it represents what has happened outside us—such as a limb being severed or a connection being broken—it is tied to a lack. The evil is in that lack, not in the mental image. — ط مد ظله

  78. The scholar Dawānī did not say that the only thing perceived is a broken connection, so it is not enough to answer that pain is a kind of direct perception and that perception is identical with what it perceives. He can say: even if direct awareness is identical with its object, we have not agreed that the only object perceived is the broken connection. That absence is perceived, as other absences are, but what we call pain is the single, present state of hurt that is felt. It is not the broken connection itself—especially when pain comes from an unhealthy bodily condition. How can that felt state be a lack? A lack, simply as a lack, has no awareness or effect, yet this painful state has both. The author himself says in his discussion of motion and rest that each thing has its own kind of existence, and that motion and relations exist in the world. If motion, relation, and other weak kinds of existence are still existents, why should pain not be an existent too? Some philosophers say pain is caused by a broken connection; others say it is caused by an unhealthy bodily state. Feeling the broken connection is awareness of the cause of pain, while feeling the hurt itself is awareness of the painful state. Since pain exists, they also question how an absence, such as a broken connection, can cause something that exists. They have tried to avoid this problem by treating the broken connection as something that exists. The true answer to Dawānī’s objection is this. What pain makes us directly aware of may be either a lack, such as a broken connection, in which case evil is a lack, as the author says; or a positive state, as the objector proposes and as we also allowed as a possibility. In that case, pain as an existing hurt is good in itself. A thing can be good in itself without being pleasant to a particular person. The fact that someone’s weakness makes a state unpleasant to them does not make it evil in itself. How could that existence be evil in its own nature when every kind of existence fits its own nature? A body calls for existence with potential multiplicity; a separate number calls for many actual units; a continuous whole calls for a connected existence; something that changes calls for an existence that changes; fire calls for an active, penetrating existence; snake venom calls for a biting, painful existence. None of these is evil in itself or by its nature. The same is true of pain. We cannot call these things evil in their own nature because a thing is evil only when it harms the existence or perfection of something already present. But here we are speaking of what each kind of thing calls for in itself from the beginning, in the fixed realities of things, which are known through God’s pure giving. There, pain is not evil in itself. It is evil only in relation to those who receive it and are affected by it. This is shown by the fact that, in God’s knowledge, which is direct and identical with what is known, pain is not called evil: God’s knowledge is active and wholly good, and He is not affected or changed. We can see that pain is called evil in our knowledge not because it is an act of awareness or an existing thing, but because it affects us and changes us. Pain also brings many further goods. It can help the blessed and those brought near to God reach high states of patience, approval, and surrender. Seeing pain also lets us understand the condition of those who suffer, so that we can help them and be helped. These benefits, as well as its existence, show that the argument needs to be answered by the distinction given here. — س قده

  79. The author uses three claims to show that pain is a lack like a broken connection: first, that awareness of what opposes us is direct, not through a mental image; second, that a thing’s existence is identical with what it is; and third, that knowledge of a thing is identical with the thing known in itself. Even if all three claims are true, they answer only one of the two perceptions: awareness of the broken connection, not the pain caused by it. The objection assumes that the two can occur separately. The real answer is the one given here: pain and hurt are positive things that exist, and are good in themselves, even when they are unpleasant to the person who feels them. — س قده

  84. The author may have realized that tracing evil to absence would mean that it occurs in every possible essence, since an essence can be the source of absences and losses. It would also mean that evil occurs at every level of existence: each lower level lacks some perfection of the level above it. So it seems that evil must be more common than good in the order of creation. He replies that the “evil” discussed here, in the agreed technical sense, means the absence of a thing or one of its perfections. A thing must have the potential to be absent, or to lose its perfection, and that is matter. Evil is therefore found only in the material world. But defining the word this way does not solve the real problem. The analysis still seems to show that absence and evil exist at levels beyond matter. The author has repeatedly said that possibility, essence, every lack, and every limit are privative in nature, and that absence is evil. The sounder answer is to admit that possible existence always includes a kind of evil, though some evil is only relative: for example, a possible thing is lacking when compared with the Necessary Existent, and each level of existence is lacking when compared with the level above it. This kind of lack is part of what the thing is and does not come from divine decree. A different kind of lack, such as death or losing a perfection after having it, is limited to matter. The author answers that kind in the main text. — ط مد ظله

Evil is the loss of a stage or limit in the moving matter, when compared with that matter’s continuing potential. This loss is a necessary part of change; it is not separately caused. Someone may object that the Shaykh’s words, “it reaches it as its destined share,” mean that destiny is the known forms within the heavenly souls, not actual things in matter: the thing that comes to be is not the same as what it comes from. Tusi answers by saying that the connection is indirect, through causes that come before it in time. There may also be a direct chain of higher causes. Perhaps Tusi is hinting at the truth as he sees it: that God has direct knowledge of particular things. — س قده

  91. Tusi’s words seem to raise two problems. First, destiny was defined as each thing’s detailed existence in matter, but intellectual substances are not in matter. How, then, can they be in both decree and destiny once? Second, decree was defined earlier as all the intellectual forms of things flowing from God at once into the world of intellects. If so, decree applies to intellectual substances, not destiny.

    The answer is that “decree” and “destiny” may be used here in broader or different senses. All intellectual substances may exist together in God’s knowledge: as a whole they are known simply, which is decree, and in all their detail, which is destiny. Or “intellectual substances” may mean intellects other than the First Intellect; the “world of intellects” in Tusi’s explanation may mean that First Intellect, which holds all their forms together in a simple way. The forms are one there in their simplicity, but their different natures can also be distinguished. This use of “destiny” is not the usual technical one.

    It is not difficult to understand intellectual substances as being in decree or destiny, since a thing may be “in” something in different senses. Motion is in time in one sense, and time is in motion in another. Their existence in both realms at once may mean that the difference is in how they are known, not in the things known. Bodily things, by contrast, are present in decree as a whole in the world of intellects, and separately in destiny in the material world, because matter has a strong hold on them. Their detailed bodily existence is different from their unified existence in the world of intellects.

    The terms may also be used in their standard senses, if we understand the eternal archetypes as part of the world of created intellects. The relation of changing things to the unchanging is timeless, so they are present in both realms together in an eternal sense. When the whole that contains all parts is considered, the separate parts have no independent status. Bodily substances, however, are considered together with their matter and are not contained in what is above them. Their detailed material existence is therefore a second kind of existence, different from their unified existence in the intellectual world.

    As the author of The Judgments says, “Intellectual substances exist in decree and destiny once, because they exist only in eternity, but from two points of view: as a whole and in detail. Bodily forms and qualities exist in both realms twice: once in eternity as a whole, and once in the endless sequence of time in detail.” This may seem compressed, but the explanation is as given above. — س قده

  92. Another way to put the argument is this: if no evil occurred in the material world—if forms never decayed or changed and never lost a later perfection—then every good would necessarily come to be and become actual. There would be no possibility of losing either an earlier or a later perfection. Matter would therefore disappear, material things would become immaterial, and every immaterial kind would exist in only one individual. The question “Why did God not create a material world without evil?” would then mean “Why did God not make do with an immaterial world, instead of creating a material world that contains evil?” The answer is that the material world contains much good. This also shows that happiness, benefit, obedience, reward, and the like could have no meaning unless misery, harm, disobedience, punishment, and their opposites were also possible. — ط مد

  96. This refers to explaining reward and punishment as the results of actions. There is another answer: apart from whether divine decree applies to them, the difference between voluntary actions and actions done under compulsion or necessity is self-evident. In fact, decree applying to an action as voluntary confirms its voluntariness; otherwise, what was decreed would fail to occur, which is impossible in God’s decree. The author seems to confuse being subject to God’s ordering with being compelled. A voluntary act, precisely as voluntary, is subject to God’s ordering: God wills it and it necessarily occurs.   97. This is what the religious teaching calls the embodiment of deeds: repeated actions give rise to settled traits, and these traits, by the permission of the all-powerful Creator, shape forms. Traits therefore cast shadows and take forms that resemble them: the greedy trait, for example, takes the form of ants; the harmful trait, the forms of snakes and scorpions. The rest can be understood by analogy. Well said:

    If a thorn has wounded you, you planted it yourself; if you wear silk, you spun its thread yourself.

  98. The objector is Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi. — ط مد ظله

  99. The charge that philosophers deny rational good and evil is a slander. How could those who are children and offspring of reason deny that reason can judge actions? The confusion comes from the objectors’ belief that philosophers define good and evil only as agreement with, or opposition to, a purpose or interest. Since they think philosophers deny purpose, they accuse them of denying good and evil too—as though they meant that a wise person should deny them.

    This question has long been disputed, so it is useful to set out the main views. Philosophers, the Imamis, and the Muʿtazilites say that good and evil are known by reason; the Ashʿarites say they are known only through religious law. The Muʿtazilites themselves differ. The earliest say actions are good or evil in themselves, not because of qualities in them. Some early thinkers say that a real quality causes both goodness and badness. Abu al-Husayn holds this only for badness: goodness needs no special quality, but badness does. Al-Jubba’i says actions are not good or evil because of real qualities, but because of points of view and relations; an act can change its moral character with the circumstances, as when striking an orphan is either discipline or abuse.

    To say that good and evil are rational means that reason can recognise that one action is truly praiseworthy and another blameworthy, even without a revealed law; or that reason can understand why an action is good and the law commands it, or why it is bad and the law forbids it. Not understanding the reasons for every action does not refute this view. We know in general that a wise person should not command or forbid an action that has no benefit or harm.

    To say that good and evil are religious means that reason cannot know whether an action is good or bad, whether its doer deserves praise or blame, or what makes any action good or bad, either before or after revelation. Another definition says that the rational view means an action really contains a feature that makes it good or bad, whether or not reason can recognise it; the religious view denies this. On the rational view, religious law reveals and explains a goodness or badness that is already true of the action. The law cannot command an action and forbid that same action at the same time, though it can do so at different times, as when a ruling is abrogated. On the religious-only view, the law itself makes an action good or bad; it does not reveal a quality that was already there. The reversals just mentioned are possible, and there is no necessary connection between prayer and entering paradise, or between wrongfully consuming an orphan’s property and consuming fire within. On that view, God could send a faithful, devoted worshipper to hell and an unbeliever to paradise. The sounder view instead holds that a necessary connection, known by reason, links good actions to delightful forms and evil actions to painful forms. The Qur'an says, “As a reward for what you used to do,” and, “As a reward for what you used to earn”; the Prophet says, “They are only your deeds, returned to you.” So the claim that cause and effect are unrelated and that God merely acts by habit is false.

    The truth is that good and evil are rational, as we know necessarily that justice and kindness deserve praise, and oppression and aggression deserve blame. Every rational person knows this, even without following a religion. Those who deny revelation, such as the Brahmins, judge this way too. Also, judging that what God commands is good and what He forbids is bad presupposes that lying is bad and that God does not lie, and that commanding what is bad or forbidding what is good is foolish and unworthy of Him. If these judgements come from reason, then reason is not shut out; if they come from revelation, the argument goes in a circle. — س قده

    ↩

  100. Since God acts with prior knowledge and approval, and no one above Him forces Him to act or competes with Him, He acts freely. The necessity philosophers speak of—“a thing does not exist until its existence is necessary”—is a necessity understood from the existence He bestows on possible effects. It is impossible to turn that into a necessity imposed on God, making Him compelled to act. — ط مد

    ↩

  101. The reply seems at first to be an argument that silences the objector, but it can be understood as a demonstration. There are two ways to make the point. First, when we ask an agent why they acted, especially if harm followed, we are asking about the compelling benefit that made the action worthwhile despite its harmful consequences. The principles and rules by which we judge our own actions are abstracted from the world’s actual order. Asking about a motive is asking about the order that made the action appropriate. Our actions follow a benefit; that benefit follows the actual order. God’s act is the actual order itself, and the benefit or wisdom we identify follows from it, as an attribute follows from what it belongs to. There is no point in asking God to make His action fit some benefit: His action is the measure of every benefit and the source from which it is understood. Nothing stands above Him to judge Him or His action.

    Second, an agent is answerable for an action only when it involves something that does not belong to them. We ask about an action when it may or may not be within their control. God owns everything in every respect, so nothing He does lies outside His ownership. This does not erase good and evil, make benefit irrelevant, or allow arbitrary action. On this account, an action is good because it belongs to the agent in a way that agrees with benefit. God’s act—the existence that comes from Him—is itself beneficial, so it belongs to Him and is good in itself. To will what is good and beneficial is not arbitrary. One may still ask what the wisdom or benefit in a particular divine act is, meaning one may seek detailed knowledge of it after knowing generally that it has a benefit. But one cannot ask whether there is any benefit at all. — ط مد

    ↩

  104. Those who believe in eternal punishment can answer the argument by choosing either option. If a person leaves human nature and becomes a new kind through their habits, that new form is a settled trait whose true nature is attachment to matter and aversion to holiness. Once the person takes on that form and its effects appear, the soul leaves the body and the truth of the matter is revealed. The effects that follow from the soul’s own nature then cause it pain, with no way to avoid them. They are perfections that suit it, but they are painful because the person now sees what they truly are. This is like someone who has developed a harmful habit that undermines life, then learns its danger only after the habit has taken hold: while doing the act, they suffer from the very thing they enjoy.

    If the person remains human in nature, the painful conditions that torment them are forced upon them, but none is everlasting or occurs for most of the time. They recur and change, as one torment interacts with another, while the soul continues along its path of misery and becomes more miserable without end. This is suggested by the verses, “Whenever its flames die down, We increase them,” and, “Whenever their skins are burned away, We replace them with other skins so that they may taste the punishment.” In short, the torment is a kind of compulsion, but the kind of torment may continue forever even though no particular torment does. The philosophers do not deny that a kind of compulsion may last forever or occur most of the time; the author himself says so when explaining why the earth is continually forced into an uneven shape, though its natural shape is a sphere. — ط مد

  105. The answer that comes to my mind now is to choose that the person remains in the original human nature. The objector says that this nature was hidden by temporary, accidental conditions. This matter is among the secrets that most minds cannot understand, and that may harm and destroy them. It is reported that the Messenger of God once passed through a street in Medina with his companions. A woman asked them to enter her house. They saw a blazing fire, with her children playing around it. She said, “Prophet of God, is God more merciful to His servants than I am to my children?” He replied, “God is the Most Merciful of those who show mercy.” She asked, “Would you ever want me to throw my child into the fire? How, then, would God put His servants into it, when He is more merciful to them?” The narrator says that the Messenger of God wept and said, “This is how God has revealed it to me.” — س قده

  115. You might say that neither this explanation nor what follows explains why living animals eat the bodies of other living animals. So the incidental urging of living animals to eat other living animals is negligible beside the protection and care given to their bodies, and the direct provision of carcasses for food.   117. The plant soul continually uses its powers to grow, nourish, strengthen, and balance its own matter—its taste, smell, and other qualities—so that it can provide material for the animal soul. Likewise, the animal soul continually prepares its own matter for the human soul. Through its powers of sense and movement, it seeks what suits it and avoids what does not, preparing its matter so that it may come to your door and enter your presence. Attar points to this when he says: “The angels’ service is all for you; paradise and hell are the reflections of your kindness and severity.” — س قده

    ↩

  118. This is how things are in reality. From the longing soul’s point of view, and according to what it senses, it may seem an advantage, a perfection, or a low and harmful state. If it does not recognise what is truly sought, who is sought, and at least what manifestation or appearance is being sought, it loses out: it confines absolute light and pure beauty to the receiver, unaware of the reality and occupied with its outward form. This way of seeing gives rise to multiplicity. When reality appears and borrowed forms disappear—as God says, “The Real has come, and falsehood has vanished,” and, “When he came to it, he found it to be nothing, but found God there”—then the person is left empty-handed and cries, “Alas for what I neglected in relation to God!” — س قده

    ↩

  119. This is voluntary death, not natural death. If the wording is left unrestricted, it could include natural separation as well. The latter kind of ascent is not possible, since this world alone is the field in which to sow: wheat yields wheat, barley yields barley. — س قده

  120. This needs qualification. The sinful aspect of actions is privative. Every sinful act has a corresponding act of the same kind that is obedience; what distinguishes them is that one agrees with a religious or rational command and the other disobeys or abandons it. Adultery and marriage, taking another’s property by force or with consent, and killing unjustly or in lawful retaliation are examples. The disobedience and abandonment are the sinful aspect of the act, and they are absences, not existing things. This is why the Qur'an generally attributes things to creation and goodness, but attributes disobedience to evil and calls it wrongdoing: “God is the Creator of everything,” “Who perfected everything He created,” and, “How evil is the name of disobedience after faith.” Perhaps the author means that the acts described as sins exist, as the end of his argument suggests when he traces blame for gossip and adultery to disobeying a command and abandoning obedience. — ط مد

  121. This is the meaning behind the saying: “A point moved lengthwise and became a line; the line moved sideways and became a surface; the surface moved in depth and became a body.” It is an image for what was described: the flowing point draws all things, just as the flowing instant draws time, and the middle movement draws the completed movement. Each of the three is like a spirit for what it draws. This is because everything is a sign of the Real, as the verse says: “In everything there is a sign that He is One.” Because the comparison might mislead, the author immediately adds a statement of transcendence, following the way the Qur'an joins these two claims: “Nothing is like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.” — س قده

    ↩

  122. This is the familiar proof that each immaterial kind is confined to one individual. It applies to the immaterial intellects in the descending order, but not to the other beings—such as the souls of the spheres and stars, and their bodies—because these are connected with matter. — ط مد

    ↩

  123. We discussed the Platonic Forms and this principle in Volume I. The account here of the order of creation—the souls and bodies of the spheres and stars, and their benefits and perfections—is based on the views of earlier astronomers and natural philosophers. Modern research does not confirm it. Since these detailed questions do not fall under general philosophical demonstrations, philosophy took them from related sciences as established assumptions. Now that they have been shown false or inadequate, the right course is to use the findings of modern research as assumptions and build the discussion on them. Those sciences are responsible for establishing their details. But the central claim—that the order of origination displays the most careful making and noblest arrangement—stands firm. The immaterial world reflects the divine order, the best and noblest order, and is more complete than what lies below it. The imaginal world reflects the intellectual world, which contains the fullest possible existence and noblest order, and is more complete than the material world below it. The material world—with its galaxies, suns, planets, and moons; their movements and cycles of generation and decay; its elements, their compounds, and their atoms; the fixed suns and moving planets within them; its particular systems and the universal order governing all of them according to constant principles, unchanging measures, and enduring guidance—all of this astonishes the mind with its beauty and fills the inner vision with its radiance. The wonders of creation, subtle care, and forms of good that human beings have discovered are only a drop in a vast ocean. — ط مد

    ↩

  124. The rays that descend from the sun to earth may travel in a straight line, reflect back along another line, or bend along a different line, forming an angle. Some rays fall on the waters around the earth and bend toward land. For example, when the sun is in the east, some of its rays reach the earth directly while others bend toward it, because the upper northern quarter of the earth is exposed above the water, while its lower northern quarter and both southern quarters are covered by water. — س قده

    ↩

  125. Every moving thing may fail to reach one end when considered from one point of view, yet reach an end when considered in relation to the causes and capacities that lead it there. That is the end its mover actually directs it toward. Each being turns toward one of God’s names and worships it; only the perfect human being, the greatest gate and straightest path, worships God in the fullest sense. A supposed failure to reach an end is relative to some other end that partial, imaginative minds expect, and that expectation is only imagined. A being can reach the highest end by coming to the threshold of this greatest gate. The Qur'an says, “This Qur'an guides to what is most upright,” and, “Enter houses by their doors.” + +Likewise, the claim that a human life naturally lasts one hundred and twenty years means that a natural kind is realized when at least one individual realizes it. Individuals with weaker constitutions and less balanced bodily conditions have a natural lifespan suited to their own matter and circumstances. To say they did not reach their “natural lifespan” means only that they did not reach the lifespan expected of the kind in an individual who lives longer. It is a relative and imagined comparison. The same applies to movements toward ends: expecting every individual to attain the highest end is based on the kind or class, not the individual, and is only an imagined expectation. Understand this well. — س قده

The explanation is that the argument seeks to establish the unity of the act, after establishing the unity of the agent and the end. If another world were proposed, it would have the same single, necessary cause; when viewed in that light, it would simply be this world, especially since we have already seen that the answer to “What is it?” is the same as the answer to “Why is it?” — س قده

If the answer to “Why?” is the same for both, then the answer to “What?” is also the same, and they are alike in kind. — س قده

  131. Every complete being includes the perfections of all that lies beneath it. After God, the First Intellect is the world’s form, its face and unity, and what brings it into actuality. Since it is simple reality, it must contain all the lower forms of existence in a unified way; the world is the place where that unity is unfolded into multiplicity. We have already learned that a kind is defined by its last and decisive feature, while the other defining elements prepare for it. What was first a condition becomes, in the end, a condition of completion. A thing is what it is through its form. The First Intellect is therefore the final defining feature and form of the Great Human: what makes it actual. A thing is also what it is through its completeness; what is incomplete is contained within what is complete, just as intellect is contained within the light of the Light of Lights. — س قده

The first interpretation is clearest. — س قده

  133. If you ask about the truth, every work of God is subtle and every form of nature is a wonder. But because we perceive these things gradually, we do not marvel at all of them. Also, when something exceeds a limit, it can have the opposite effect. The signs, proofs, and wonders have become so numerous that people no longer notice them. Each being, by virtue of its own nature, can do something or several things that others cannot. The complete human being alone is more wondrous than all wonders. One of our leaders is reported to have said: “The Holy Spirit in the gardens of the celestial sphere has tasted the first fruits of our gardens.” If this is the state of the Holy Spirit, what do you think the state of others is? You can see the truth of what we have said about the presence of wondrous signs if you return each existing thing to its first state: a shapeless material or an inert element, without any decoration or form. Compare that first, empty state with what has been adorned and completed by its first and later perfections, and you will see the difference between the head of a gathering beneath domes and dust, between the Lord of lords and earth. Then even the movement of the lowly earthworm becomes a wonder, and understanding it a greater wonder. The flight of a fly, which resists the air, is strange; stranger still is its care in touching its head and wings with its legs and cleaning them so they do not get dirty or weigh it down and prevent it from flying. If these things are so wondrous, what of the nobler beings—and especially the noblest being, the human being, who once passed through a time when he was nothing worth mentioning, a dirty drop and impure blood, then changed through stages into an embryo and grew until he came out of his mother’s womb, still one of the weakest creatures? He then grew to maturity and learned to distinguish guidance from error. If God’s care reaches him, he may become a person who knows God, a powerful angel, a leader who displays knowledge and power, a saint, or a prophet and God’s deputy. In the end, he gathers beings into himself, inherits them, and folds them into his own existence, just as the First Intellect is God’s deputy, giving existence to beings according to their readiness and unfolding them in their kinds at the beginning. If you are amazed, this is what is most amazing; if you are moved, this is what is most moving. So rise and sing along with the nightingale in the sanctuary of love and the songbird in the gardens of knowledge and guidance: “The unseen voice pours wine into our cup; let the musician play, for the world has gone our way. We have seen the beloved’s face reflected in the cup, though you know nothing of the pleasure of drinking without end. We delight in the eyes of our beloved; for this reason, our reins have been handed over to intoxication.” This visible human being and the wonder he displays are described in the verse of the author’s spiritual guide. — س قده

  148. The active principles and powers are angels insofar as they are connected to what is above them. They are like His seeing eyes and working hands, or levels of His active power. Since the questioner’s words suggested that a single task would be a lowly state, the author first establishes the angels’ nobility, then shows that many actions can issue from them in an ordered sequence. The universal intellects and souls—the angels brought near, who stand in rows and direct affairs—have many actions in this way. The active principles in the imaginal world do too.   154. The animal souls meant here are those on the path toward human beings, since something is adorned by what is connected to it. Natural powers reflect his nature; plants his plant life; animals his animal life; embryos and devils his capacity for cunning; working angels his practical reason, purity, and protection from sin; and angels who know his theoretical reason, wisdom, and knowledge. The sphere, which the divine Book calls “smoke,” reflects his vital spirit, form, and beauty. In short, the powers and natures of all the worlds are gathered within him in a unified way. A Persian verse says: “When we sent Adam out, we spread our beauty across the plain.”

  157. It is easy to understand how sound might exist in the heavens, through bodies striking or touching one another as they move. As for tastes and pleasant scents, the author has hinted at how they may be there: whoever gives a perfection must possess it. Yet other beings do not receive these qualities by tasting or smelling them as we do. The clearer account is that, if God made them reach such a being, it would become a sphere—unless this were done as a miracle for a prophet. Such a being would then possess what it received, because the spheres act upon things made from the elements and have stronger active powers than fire. Another explanation, which the philosophers in Aristotle’s school would accept if they listened, is that the spheres possess these bodily perfections in a higher way, through the forms in their senses—their own inward images. These forms are present through active knowing, not passive reception, just as a human soul may create the image of a beautiful face in its shared sense even when the body it inhabits does not have a beautiful face. A scholar would judge that this person possesses the beautiful image in a higher and more complete way than the matter in which it is impressed. The ignorant person would not, because he did not see the beauty on the body. The same applies to taste, smell, and other senses. Since the spheres perceive through strong, active knowing, the author holds that their inward images are senses, as our imagination is a sense. The sphere itself, however, is simple, with similar parts, so it cannot contain different powers and natures in the way a body does. — س قده

  162. This is taken from the noble traditions: the Inhabited House is truly the place where God is remembered and known. It is the station of the souls in heaven, that is, in their matter and form. — س قده

  163. The first group are the universal intellects sought by the movements of the heavens. They are compared to the heavens. Their prostration is their complete disappearance and erasure in witnessing the transcendent Real. The second group are the universal and particular souls impressed in matter, which seek the universal intellects as manifestations of God and His overpowering lights. They bow because their existence has not vanished as completely as that of the first group; they are also directed toward the heavenly bodies. From this, a worshipper should reflect on the meanings of the postures in prayer. A Persian verse says: “Every veil He draws has a path within it.” In standing, one leaves attachment to the natural world and follows no passing desire; one rises from worldly life, stands before God, and affirms the oneness of His actions. In bowing, one lowers oneself, surrenders, and stretches out one’s neck as if ready to be struck, submitting to God’s words: “God has bought the believers’ lives in exchange for the garden”—the garden of attributes or the garden of the divine essence. The one who bows affirms the oneness of God’s attributes. In prostration, one’s existence disappears and is erased completely, affirming the oneness of God’s essence and passing away fully in Him. — س قده

    ↩

  164. That is, God formed the body and also shaped the inward soul in all forty-eight familiar forms. Some thinkers of illumination say that the body, like the soul, is impressed with the forms of things. — س قده

  165. People are kept from this knowledge by turning away from divine philosophy and mathematical sciences, especially astronomy, the noblest of them. They know the heavens only as a color and the stars only as glints and flashes. In truth, they know nothing of the heavens: the color they see belongs to vapour and smoke. They have no understanding of what the heavens are, whether they exist, why they exist, what matter, form, and the fifth nature mean, or what their individual and universal souls are. They have shown no sign of understanding because their concerns are food, sex, and power over people in the natural world. They have not reflected on the creation of the heavens or themselves, or on their greatness, which would make worldly things seem small. They have not reflected on the lasting realm of the spirit, or how short a thousand years of bodily life is compared with the soul’s continued life—whether it is blessed and delighted by meeting God or tormented and deprived. A finite period cannot be compared with what has no end. The same is true when you compare the greatness of your holy soul with the greatness of the world: a person who has never seen a mountain thinks a camel is enormous, while someone who sees the camel beside the mountain knows how small it is.

    Raise your luminous imagination to the spheres and look with astonishment at the quarter of the earth that lies uncovered by water, and at the tiny creatures crawling over it. That is how created beings look from above. Why do people cling to the earth and boast of owning it? How small it is, and how small are those who control it, compared with the vast spheres and their countless stars. Many stars are each larger than the whole earth. Look inwardly at their immense sizes, not as they appear to your outward sight—as small, dim points of light. Notice their varied movements: some travel westward against the usual order, others eastward with it; their speeds differ too. Some complete a circuit in a year, others in twelve years, others in thirty years. The slowest takes twenty-five thousand two hundred years, while the fastest completes its circuit in twenty-four hours. Others take different lengths of time. Notice how the fixed stars keep their positions in relation to one another, while the wandering stars continually change position. They are manifestations of God’s enduring life and displays of His power and care.

    Then rise in your mind to the world of their individual souls, the imagination of the Great Human, whose body is the spheres and all they contain; then to their universal souls, which perceive universal and separate realities; and then to the universal intellects and overpowering lights, both those in a vertical order and those spread across one level. They are simple beings that encompass all, each a unified whole. Whoever sees them has seen God, for they belong to the divine realm. Divine qualities prevail in them, and the rules of everything other than God are consumed within them: they have no state of waiting or readiness to receive. Then follow the poet’s counsel: “O bird’s egg of possibility, you are both the white and the yolk. Spread your wings and fly beyond this old, worn sky.” Be one of those who swim in the sea of God’s greatness and stand in rows before Him, with steadiness and a firm station. The stages of completion are attachment, taking on divine qualities, and realization—or, if you prefer, a passing thought, a state, a settled trait, and a firm station. “Remain upright, as you have been commanded.” — س قده

    ↩

In beings that can act, movement is the means by which the agent reaches its goal. It is like a necessary step toward a goal: needed to get there, but not the goal itself. — س قده

  170. The first point gives every being a beloved; the second says that all existence is one reality, so that the beloved of all beings is God. Each being longs for its perfection, and its perfection belongs to the same order as itself: strong whiteness completes weak whiteness, for example, not blackness; strong light and heat complete weak light and heat, not their opposites. We have established that existence does not consist of wholly separate realities. — س قده

  171. This may be a slip of the pen. Certainty is knowledge that something must be so and that its opposite cannot be so. It is general and lasting, and no proof can remove it.   173. In everyday speech, “love” often means the special attachment between male and female animals: desire for sexual union. All beauty, goodness, and happiness return to existence, just as their opposites return to non-existence. This kind of attachment is found between every level of existence and what is above it, between a being and itself, and between a being and the perfections that follow from it. So love must run through all beings, whether or not we say that life and awareness run through them too. This shows that love does not mean knowledge or awareness, though the two may be found together. The author’s claim that love without life or awareness is only a name may therefore need review. — T. M. (editor).

  174. The author has proved that knowledge goes with existence apart from matter. Matter, and material things such as bodies, cannot be present to themselves in this way, so they are not directly knowing subjects or objects of knowledge. Knowing them means knowing them through their imaginal and intellectual forms. The same account applies to power: active power means that something can produce effects. In material things, this means that their imaginal and intellectual forms are the sources of their effects, since bodily power is only the possibility of acting, not its full activity. If knowledge and power run through all beings, so does life, which means that a being can know and act. — T. M. (editor).

  178. First, the connection described here is a special one: it is attachment to perfection and completion, as we have indicated. Relations and connections, if they are abstract notions, are like these attributes. If they are real relations of existence, they are like the other kinds of existence in which we find love. All of them are dependent existences in relation to the Necessary Being, as every effect is in relation to its cause. If Ibn Sina means relations in the formal sense, they are real accidents. To object to his claim that love runs through accidents by citing surfaces and edges, when he himself says that love runs through them, is to rely on a claim the other side does not accept.   180. That is, there is nothing separate from God, standing apart from Him. All existence is His manifestation, its link to Him, and complete dependence on Him.   181. You might object that preserving effects through the love of their cause requires the higher cause to attend to the lower effect. New things also arise through His love for Himself, the fixed realities’ love for His names, essences’ love for their existence, and beings’ love for their perfection.   182. Just as the cause loves the effect’s perfection through its love for itself, the effect also loves the cause indirectly, because whoever loves what something requires also loves the thing itself. The effect’s perfection is preserved by love in this way: the cause loves itself. The effect’s being is preserved through the love that follows from that first love. Another reading is that every effect is preserved by the effect’s love for its cause, because a thing is what it is through its completeness and perfection. As the author will say, loving its cause means that its being is linked to the cause. This real being is the bond of existence, its connection to the cause, and the outpouring of existence from the cause to it. This link is a form of love: the author calls it will, connection, and love, as in the saying, “I loved to be known.” Love, will, and connection are one. Through this dependent existence, the effect keeps its identity, since it is nothing but a relation. Without this link, it would have no identity. If the lower being did not love the higher—that is, depend on it—it would vanish. If “love” instead means the love the higher being has for the perfection of the lower, that is the higher being’s love for itself, as we have seen. — س قده

  196. God says: “Your creation and your rising again are like the creation and raising of a single soul.” Each material part changes form and receives a new one, because God’s giving never stops and His light never sets. A Persian verse says: “By His power, in the field of timeless dominion, each breath becomes Abraham’s fire, each handful of dust a human being.” Traditions from the Imams say that there is no place on earth that has not been a human being’s grave. This does not conflict with all beings eventually reaching their highest goal at the great Resurrection, when the world changes. That account describes a vertical order, as we see in the complete human being: even the body changes toward its final goal. The elements that once received its light can still continue moving; they are not left without purpose. Each thing has a container suited to it. Since the possible things and their goals are without end, there are many movements, also without end: positional and non-positional, accidental and substantial, sideways and upward, in endless containers.   198. They may see no stronger reason than this love to draw the soul away from the desires of the natural world after it has been drawn toward God or has followed religious discipline. You may object that spiritual teachers must reconcile religious law with the spiritual path, and that the most learned among them hold firmly to this principle. How can it agree with religious law? Perhaps they found permission in its symbols and subtle meanings. Or perhaps they allowed one act to be both commanded and forbidden, as many religious scholars do. For example, leaving a house wrongfully occupied is commanded, but the act also involves using another person’s property without permission. Removing the penis after adultery is commanded, but the act is also forbidden for the same reason. The same act is therefore both forbidden and required from different points of view. A fuller explanation belongs elsewhere. God knows the secrets. — س قده

  221. Here the author follows later logicians, who focus on the surface form of words and set competing expressions against one another. This turns the opposition between affirmation and denial—the most basic and obvious principle—into a difficult theory that a student can understand only with great effort. The author’s heading for the subject, “the opposition between affirmation and denial,” is much clearer than the explanation he adds. The earlier logicians were right: the most basic principle is that affirmation and denial cannot both be true and cannot both be false of the same claim. Put another way, a claim and its denial cannot both be true or both false. In truth, this opposition is between a positive and negative statement. Single terms contradict only because their meanings lead back to a positive or negative statement, such as “Zayd exists” and “Zayd does not exist.” — T. M. (editor).

    ↩

  222. The author’s account implies that denial is the direct opposite of affirmation, but affirmation is not the direct opposite of denial, since affirmation does not itself mean “removing” or “denying.” It is the result of denying a denial. So the opposition would be between a direct opposite and something that follows from the opposite. But it is obvious that affirmation itself directly excludes denial; it does not need to do so by following from a second denial. This is enough to show the weakness of that explanation. Affirmation and denial are directly opposed, so there can be no middle ground between them. — T. M. (editor).

This means that “the denial of a denial contradicts a denial” really means that it contradicts the positive statement that follows from the denial. Every positive statement has a direct opposite, its denial; a denial has no direct opposite of its own, only a positive statement that follows from it. — T. M. (editor).

  233. By “a thing” he means a respect or feature. For example, if we say that the First Intellect is the source of a particular sphere because of its relation to the Necessary Being, that relation is an explanatory respect. If we say that it is the source because it is possible in itself, that is a defining respect. The point is not that the thing itself is a cause or effect; that would make the respect part of the thing. A cause is a cause through what makes it able to cause. In the case of God, who is cause through Himself, causality is His very being. In other causes, their ability to cause comes from a feature that makes them actual causes. That feature, in truth, is the cause. The same applies to an effect: being caused is the very being of what is made. — س قده

  234. The author’s account is unusual. In “humanity without condition,” the aspect is not truly a defining feature; it is only a way of speaking. It would be clearer to distinguish three cases. First, “without condition” can mean that we are not considering any condition as part of the subject, as in “humanity in itself is neither existent nor non-existent.” Second, a feature can be part of the subject, as in “a body, insofar as it is flat, is white” or “a body, insofar as it is white, can be seen.” Third, a feature can explain why a claim is true, as in “a human being laughs because they can understand unusual things” and “a person who is surprised laughs.” In the third case, the reason is outside the subject as such, so it does not make the subject more complex. A critic might say that surprise and understanding are themselves qualities that add to a person. They do, if they are treated as defining features. But when they are treated as reasons for a claim about the person, they are explanatory. Another might say that a cause explains the predicate, not the subject. But because the predicate and subject are joined in existence, the cause explains the subject too: being surprised explains why a human being laughs, and understanding unusual things explains why they are surprised. — س قده

  235. The truth is that a difference in meaning alone is not a real defining feature, since it does not truly restrict the thing. So it does not challenge the common view that real defining features make a thing more complex. — س قده

The truth is that existence and non-existence follow the same rule. Partial non-existence occurs when something is absent in one way; complete non-existence occurs only when it is absent in every way. Likewise, partial existence occurs when it exists in one way; complete and unrestricted existence, such as God’s existence, is present in every way and at every level. — T. M. (editor).

  244. The first term is used by the Illuminationist philosophers, the second by the philosophers in Aristotle’s school. A form is what makes a thing actual. “Dimensions” includes both material and imagined dimensions. The third term refers to separate intellects that rise to the universal intellectual world. They are the final links in the upward chain, corresponding to the universal intellects that begin the downward chain of creation. Opponents reject this insight because they think it requires the existence of something eternal and separate from God. They do not see that the real problem would be an existence separate from every essence and quality, or an independent being other than God. This light, however, belongs to God’s own realm. It is separate because God makes it so, and eternal because it depends on God’s eternity. Recognizing it does not limit God’s power: it is itself God’s power and hand. Its act, and the act of everything in God’s realm, is God’s act. Its coming from God is like the whole world’s coming from God. After the Real, all existences are its shadows, just as it is God’s shadow. “Have you not seen how your Lord extends the shadow?” — س قده

In this upward development, the soul does not cast off one form and put on another; it takes on one after another. Since a cause must be akin to its effect, and essences remain through the levels while existence is one reality whose distinguishing and shared features are the same, the higher level can contain the actualities of all lower beings in one simple way.   301. The argument depends on a special feature linking the effect to its cause. A careful commentator says that the earlier formulation better suits the language of declaring God beyond all likeness, while this one uses the words “likeness” and “similarity,” even though nothing resembles the first source. That criticism is right. The wording is awkward: it says that fit is likeness, and likeness is a kind of sameness in quality, ultimately a sameness in reality. If “likeness” and “sameness” are used in their technical senses, the argument would not apply to God or to any simple substantial cause, and the premise is itself disputed. If the words are used loosely, the added statements do no work; it would be enough to say that fit means sameness in reality. The further distinction—that sameness between two qualities is called likeness, while sameness between two subjects is called similarity—only makes the argument less clear. A better proof would say: a true cause must have an essential relation and a special bond to its effect, so that the effect’s existence depends on the cause’s existence. This bond requires a kind of shared nature between them, differing only in strength and weakness. If two things came from a truly simple One, either they would come from one aspect, making the One two, or from two aspects, making it composite. Both are impossible. — T. M. (editor).

  317. A firmer and shorter proof can be built on this premise: existence is fundamental and graded, differing in strength and weakness, actuality and potentiality, nobility and lowliness. Causation among possible beings, together with the claim that creation concerns existence itself, requires more than two levels of existence. One is necessarily God; the others are possible beings, some nobler than others. A caused existence is dependent and relational: it cannot stand by itself, but is grounded in an independent existence. Thus each essential level is dependent on the level above and supports the one below. In a three-level chain, the lowest is dependent on the middle, the middle independently supports the lowest but depends on the highest, and the highest independently supports all below it. If a lower, less noble level existed without a nobler level before it—whether the nobler level came at the same time, later, or never—then something that depends on a cause would exist without its cause, which is impossible. — T.
